Iran's monthslong internet shutdown is crushing businesses in an already battered economy

claim.statement: Independent and near-measurement sources as of 1-2 May 2026 support selective access, not public restoration: IODA said active probing fell to about 3% on 28 February and had not recovered by 27 April; CHN/KhabarOnline citing NetBlocks put the day-63 broad connectivity metric at 1-2%; and Safhe Eghtesad/CITNA said estimates above 10% mainly reflect Internet Pro, special, organizational, or non-public routes rather than ordinary-user restoration.
claim.subject: Iran global-internet connectivity
claim.object: selective special-path recovery rather than public restoration

evidence.summary: IODA reports active probing at about 3% after February 28 with no recovery, while Google/NIN and IranCell/Telescope signals point to whitelist or Internet Pro access rather than ordinary public internet.
CHN/KhabarOnline says the broad shutdown reached 1,488 hours/day 63 and cites connectivity falling to 1-2%.
Safhe Eghtesad/CITNA says the above-10% estimate is mostly in non-public, organizational, special, or Internet Pro routes, while broad NetBlocks-style measurement remains around 1-2%.
The v41 notes reconcile the apparently divergent 1-3% and 10%+ figures as different populations and access paths.

information_depth.rationale: The claim relies on IODA measurement interpretation, NetBlocks-cited near-current reporting, and an explicit Persian explanation of why special-path estimates are higher than broad national connectivity.

assessment.uncertainty: NetBlocks' direct May 1 post was found only through syndications/search excerpts, not a standalone crawled NetBlocks post. Official operator-level measurements and direct OONI/Cloudflare dashboards would further strengthen the assessment.

claim.statement: Internet Society Pulse classifies Iran's blackout as an ongoing national shutdown and describes the restoration pattern as managed and asymmetric: January 28 brought partial, patchy, heavily filtered restoration; mid-February recovered only about 50-60% of traffic; February 28 returned traffic nearly to zero; and later access was selectively re-enabled for sectors, organizations, fixed-IP allowlists, and controlled gateways rather than open consumer-level access.
claim.subject: Internet Society Pulse Iran shutdown record
claim.object: the shutdown as ongoing with managed selective restoration

evidence.summary: Internet Society Pulse lists the shutdown as ongoing, gives the January/February timeline, and summarizes selective sector/fixed-IP/allowlist recovery rather than full restoration.
The source notes compare the Pulse timeline with the IODA/NetBlocks/Safhe measurement signals.

information_depth.rationale: Pulse aggregates multiple measurement and documentation sources and explicitly distinguishes full restoration from managed/selective access.

assessment.uncertainty: Pulse includes some older January-February timeline elements; use it as an ongoing-status and pattern source, not as a minute-by-minute May 2 measurement.

claim.statement: AP reporting on 1 May 2026 ties the prolonged blackout to concrete livelihood collapse: Iran's 90m people have been cut off from the global internet for most of 2026; all global-web access is described as shut down except expensive workarounds and limited white-SIM/professional exceptions; direct losses are estimated at $30-40m per day with indirect losses potentially twice that; and about 10m jobs depend on internet connectivity.
claim.subject: Iran internet shutdown
claim.object: large daily economic and livelihood losses while preserving privileged access

evidence.summary: AP reports months of business losses, $30-40m direct daily losses, potential indirect losses twice that, 10m jobs tied to connectivity, white SIMs, limited professional access, and most users left with the national net.
Internet Society Pulse connects the shutdown to work, education, healthcare coordination, and economic disruption.

information_depth.rationale: AP combines in-country interviews, named sector estimates, and existing official/business figures; exact loss totals remain estimates.

assessment.uncertainty: The loss estimates vary across sources and depend on exchange rates and digital-economy scope.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v41 - Measurements confirm selective access, not restoration
synthesis.summary: The forty-first pass closes the measurement gap left by v40. The apparent conflict between '1-3%' and 'above 10%' connectivity is not a real contradiction. IODA says active probing fell to about 3% on February 28 and had not recovered by April 27; CHN/KhabarOnline citing NetBlocks puts the May 1/day-63 broad connectivity level at 1-2%; and Safhe Eghtesad/CITNA says estimates above 10% mainly reflect non-public routes such as Internet Pro, special access, organizational access, and specific network paths. Internet Society Pulse classifies the shutdown as ongoing and describes recovery as patchy, filtered, sector-specific, fixed-IP/allowlist-based, and not open consumer restoration. AP adds the social/economic cost: 90m people largely cut off from the global web, $30-40m in direct daily losses, possible indirect losses twice that, and about 10m jobs tied to internet connectivity, while white SIMs and limited professional access remain. Net: the measurement layer supports the same diagnosis as the policy layer: the regime has not restored ordinary public internet; it has preserved a managed exception system and allowed special-path recovery to masquerade as improvement.
synthesis.limitations: Direct May 1 NetBlocks data was found via syndications/search excerpts rather than a standalone crawled NetBlocks post. Direct OONI, Cloudflare Radar, Kentik, operator-level, and user-measurement dashboards would further strengthen granularity. Treat the 10%+ estimate as a near-primary Persian technical claim about special access, not a public-connectivity baseline.

information_depth.rationale: The synthesis combines measurement-platform interpretation, current NetBlocks-citing reporting, a Persian technical reconciliation of special-path access, AP field reporting, and v40 policy/discourse rows.

operations.rationale: The claim directly answers the rollback/restoration question using independent measurement and near-measurement evidence.
The Pulse record frames the shutdown as ongoing and the recovery as selective/managed rather than public rollback.
The shutdown's business-collapse and job-dependency numbers are a likely driver of delayed layoffs and labor stress.
The same selective-access architecture affects education and campus life through unstable/filtered connectivity.

operations.reason: v41 adds independent network-measurement evidence showing that Internet Pro/special-path recovery is not ordinary public restoration.
